# eindir

> eindir is a Rust crate, eindir-core, with Python, C and C++ bindings. It has the primitives for bounded optimisation and sampling on R^D: the Objective trait, box bounds, Halton point sets, gradients, a GLE coloured-noise thermostat and surrogate models. The anneal optimiser is built on it.

Each link points at the Org source of a page under `docs/orgmode/` on GitHub. The site, https://eindir.rgoswami.me/, is built from the same sources by Sphinx, and `llms-full.txt` has every page as Markdown in one file.

The Python package is narrower than the Rust crate. `eindir` exports `NumLimit`, `FPair`, `ObjectiveFunction`, `OutOfBounds`, `low_discrepancy_points`, `styblinski_tang` and array API, DLPack and TVM-FFI helpers, and `eindir._core` adds `Bounds`, `PyObjective` and `shifted_low_discrepancy_points`. `GleThermostat`, `optimal_sampling_drift`, `matrix_exp`, `ldl_sqrt`, `halton_unit`, the surrogates, the gradient adapters and the builtin objective types are Rust-only. CI runs the Python blocks of the manual, and the Rust code in the tutorials is included from `examples/`.

The `eindir-python` skill and the three others under `skills/` give worked examples of common tasks, with scripts that CI runs. `AGENTS.md` has the build, test and documentation commands and the mistakes that are easy to make. Both are reproduced at the end of `llms-full.txt`.

The pages follow in the order of the site's navigation, converted from Org to Markdown. The Rust API reference that Sphinx generates from the doc comments in `src/` is not included, so read the sources or run `cargo doc --open`.

## Overview

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/index.org

**eindir Documentation**

![eindir](/_static/eindir_logo.png)

### Overview

eindir has the pieces that optimisers and samplers on a box in R^D share: an objective trait with box bounds, Halton point sets, gradient adapters, a coloured-noise thermostat for the generalized Langevin equation (GLE), and surrogate models.
It is a Rust crate, `eindir-core`, with a Python package, `eindir`, and a C library with a C++ companion header.
The [anneal](https://github.com/HaoZeke/anneal) optimiser is built on it.

- Objectives: `Objective<T>` over `Bounds<T>`, with batch and parallel evaluation, and `TryObjective` for objectives that can fail.
- Point sets: Halton designs scaled to a box, with seeded shifts and corner-anchored variants.
- Gradients: the `Gradient<T>` trait, analytic and central-difference adapters, and forward-mode automatic differentiation with the `autodiff` feature.
- GLE thermostat: `GleThermostat` with a fitted drift that samples a band of frequencies evenly.
- Surrogates: an additive Chebyshev model with independence sampling, a total-degree Chebyshev polynomial, and objectives restricted to a subspace.
- Test functions: `Rastrigin`, `Rosenbrock`, `Ackley` and `StybTang2D`.

Python covers objectives, bounds and point sets; the rest is Rust-only.
The C ABI passes objectives between C and Rust, with a version stamp and a semantic descriptor to check that both sides agree.

### Where to start

- [Quickstart](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/quickstart.org) evaluates a function at well-spread points from Python and Rust.
- [Installation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/howto/install.org) covers PyPI, crates.io, source builds and the C library.
- [Objectives through the C ABI](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/howto/c-objective.org) passes a C function to Rust code.
- [Python API](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/reference/api-primitives.org) and [C API](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/reference/c-api.org) list every function; the [Rust API reference](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/reference/rust-api.org) is generated from the crate.

### Citing

Cite the software record on Zenodo, [10.5281/zenodo.10672737](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10672737); the [FAQ](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/howto/faq.org) has a BibTeX entry.
eindir is released under the MIT licence.

## Quickstart

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/quickstart.org

This page evaluates a function at eight well-spread points in a box, first from Python and then from Rust.
Both draw the same Halton points and find the same best start.

### Install

Python:

```bash
pip install eindir
```

Rust, in `Cargo.toml`:

```toml
[dependencies]
eindir-core = "0.6"
ndarray = "0.17"
```

The newest release on crates.io is 0.6.0 and on PyPI 0.5.1.
For the main branch, use `eindir-core = { git = "https://github.com/HaoZeke/eindir" }` or run `maturin develop --features python` in a checkout.
[Installation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/howto/install.org) has the other routes.

### Python

`_core.Bounds` is a box and `_core.PyObjective` wraps a Python function as an objective over it.
`eindir.low_discrepancy_points` returns Halton points in the box as an `(n, d)` array.

```python
import numpy as np
import eindir
from eindir import _core

low = np.array([-5.12, -5.12])
high = np.array([5.12, 5.12])
obj = _core.PyObjective(lambda x: float(np.sum((x - 1.0) ** 2)), _core.Bounds(low, high))

starts = eindir.low_discrepancy_points(low, high, 8)
values = [obj.eval(row) for row in starts]
best = int(np.argmin(values))
print(starts[best], values[best])
```

```text
[1.28       2.84444444] 3.480375308641971
```

`_core` takes contiguous float64 NumPy arrays only; `eindir.low_discrepancy_points` converts lists for you.

### Rust

An objective is a type that implements `Objective<f64>`: its dimension, its bounds and its value.
`eval_batch` evaluates the rows of a 2-D array.

```rust
//! A sphere objective on a 2-D box, evaluated at eight Halton start points.
//! The manual's Quickstart includes this file; `cargo run --example quickstart`.
use eindir_core::{Bounds, Objective, low_discrepancy_points};
use ndarray::{ArrayView1, array};

struct Sphere {
    bounds: Bounds<f64>,
}

impl Objective<f64> for Sphere {
    fn dim(&self) -> usize {
        self.bounds.dims
    }

    fn bounds(&self) -> &Bounds<f64> {
        &self.bounds
    }

    fn eval(&self, x: ArrayView1<f64>) -> f64 {
        x.iter().map(|xi| (xi - 1.0).powi(2)).sum()
    }
}

fn main() {
    let bounds = Bounds::new(array![-5.12, -5.12], array![5.12, 5.12], 1e-6);
    let obj = Sphere { bounds };
    let starts = low_discrepancy_points(obj.bounds(), 8, 1);
    let values = obj.eval_batch(starts.view());
    let best = (0..values.len())
        .min_by(|&a, &b| values[a].total_cmp(&values[b]))
        .unwrap();
    println!("{} {}", starts.row(best), values[best]);
}
```

```text
[1.2800000000000002, 2.844444444444443] 3.480375308641971
```

The file is `examples/quickstart.rs`, and `cargo run --example quickstart` runs it.

- [GLE thermostat](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/tutorials/gle-thermostat.org) and [Surrogates](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/tutorials/surrogates.org) are Rust-only.

## Tutorials

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/tutorials.org

The tutorials build up from the [Quickstart](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/quickstart.org).
Each one runs as written: CI runs the Python blocks of the manual, and the Rust code is included from `examples/`, which `cargo test` builds.

| Tutorial | Language | What it covers |
|---|---|---|
| [Quickstart with Python](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/tutorials/quickstart.org) | Python | An objective with a gradient, start points, the pure-Python classes |
| [Low-discrepancy points](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/tutorials/low-discrepancy.org) | Python, Rust | Halton designs, shifted replicas, corner-anchored designs |
| [GLE thermostat](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/tutorials/gle-thermostat.org) | Rust | The coloured-noise thermostat on its own |
| [Surrogates](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/tutorials/surrogates.org) | Rust | An additive surrogate, its proposals, a reduced objective |

The GLE thermostat and the surrogates have no Python binding.

To check the version of an installed package:

```python
import eindir
print(eindir._core.__version__)
```

`eindir.__version__` does not exist.

## Quickstart with Python

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/tutorials/quickstart.org

This tutorial wraps a Python function and its gradient as an objective, draws start points inside its bounds, and evaluates them.
It needs `pip install eindir` and NumPy.

### Step 1: an objective with a gradient

`_core.Bounds(low, high, slack=1e-6)` is the box.
`_core.PyObjective(fn, bounds, grad_fn=None)` wraps `fn`, which takes a 1-D float64 array and returns a float.
`grad_fn`, when given, returns the gradient as an array of the same length.

```python
import numpy as np
from eindir import _core

low = np.full(2, -5.12)
high = np.full(2, 5.12)


def rastrigin(x):
    return float(10.0 * len(x) + np.sum(x**2 - 10.0 * np.cos(2.0 * np.pi * x)))


def rastrigin_grad(x):
    return 2.0 * x + 20.0 * np.pi * np.sin(2.0 * np.pi * x)


obj = _core.PyObjective(rastrigin, _core.Bounds(low, high), grad_fn=rastrigin_grad)
print(obj.dim, obj.eval(np.zeros(2)), obj.grad(np.array([0.5, 0.0])))
```

Without `grad_fn`, `obj.grad` raises `ValueError`.
Python has no finite-difference fallback, so pass a gradient or difference the function yourself.

### Step 2: start points

`eindir.low_discrepancy_points(low, high, n, skip=1)` returns `n` Halton points in the box.
The same arguments always give the same points, so a run can be repeated exactly.

```python
import numpy as np
import eindir
from eindir import _core

low = np.full(2, -5.12)
high = np.full(2, 5.12)
obj = _core.PyObjective(
    lambda x: float(20.0 + np.sum(x**2 - 10.0 * np.cos(2.0 * np.pi * x))),
    _core.Bounds(low, high),
)

starts = eindir.low_discrepancy_points(low, high, 8)
values = np.array([obj.eval(row) for row in starts])
print(starts.shape, values.min())
assert np.all((starts >= low) & (starts <= high))
```

### Step 3: the pure-Python classes

`eindir.NumLimit` and `eindir.ObjectiveFunction` are plain Python and separate from `_core`.
A subclass of `ObjectiveFunction` implements `singlepoint`, `multipoint` and `__repr__`; calling it counts calls in `.calls`.

```python
import numpy as np
import eindir


class Sphere(eindir.ObjectiveFunction):
    def singlepoint(self, pos):
        return float(np.sum(pos**2))

    def multipoint(self, pos):
        return np.sum(pos**2, axis=-1)

    def __repr__(self):
        return "Sphere"


limits = eindir.NumLimit(low=np.full(2, -1.0), high=np.full(2, 1.0), dims=2)
f = Sphere(limits)
print(f(np.array([0.5, 0.5])), f(np.array([[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 0.0]])), f.calls)
```

Pass `dims` to `NumLimit`: it defaults to 1, and `ObjectiveFunction` uses it to tell one point from many.

### Where to go next

The GLE thermostat, the surrogates and the gradient adapters are Rust-only; see [GLE thermostat](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/tutorials/gle-thermostat.org) and [Surrogates](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/tutorials/surrogates.org).
[Using with anneal](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/howto/using-with-anneal.org) shows where these objects go in the anneal drivers.

## Low-discrepancy points

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/tutorials/low-discrepancy.org

This tutorial draws Halton point sets in a box: a plain design, shifted replicas of it and a design that starts at the corners.
[Low-discrepancy point sets](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/explanation/low-discrepancy.org) explains the construction.

### Python

`eindir.low_discrepancy_points(low, high, n, skip=1)` returns an `(n, d)` NumPy array.
Row `r` is Halton point `skip + r` scaled to the box, so `skip=1` leaves out the corner `low` that point 0 maps to.

```python
import numpy as np
import eindir

low = np.array([-5.12, -5.12])
high = np.array([5.12, 5.12])

starts = eindir.low_discrepancy_points(low, high, 16)
print(starts.shape, starts[0])
assert np.all((starts >= low) & (starts <= high))

# skip continues the sequence: rows 8.. of one call are rows 0.. of the next.
more = eindir.low_discrepancy_points(low, high, 8, skip=9)
assert np.allclose(more, starts[8:])
```

`eindir._core.shifted_low_discrepancy_points(low, high, n, skip=1, seed=0)` adds a random shift modulo 1 to every point before scaling, with the shift drawn from `seed`.
It returns a list of rows, not an array.

```python
import numpy as np
from eindir import _core

low = np.array([-5.12, -5.12])
high = np.array([5.12, 5.12])

a = np.asarray(_core.shifted_low_discrepancy_points(low, high, 16, 1, 3))
b = np.asarray(_core.shifted_low_discrepancy_points(low, high, 16, 1, 3))
c = np.asarray(_core.shifted_low_discrepancy_points(low, high, 16, 1, 4))
assert np.array_equal(a, b) and not np.array_equal(a, c)
print(a.shape)
```

Unlike `eindir.low_discrepancy_points`, the `_core` function takes contiguous float64 arrays only.

### Rust

The Rust crate also has `halton_unit` for one point in the unit cube and `boundary_anchored_low_discrepancy_points`, which puts the corners and the centre of the box first when there is room for them.

```rust
//! Halton designs in a box: the plain design, a seeded shifted replica and a
//! design anchored at the corners. The low-discrepancy tutorial includes
//! this file; `cargo run --example low_discrepancy`.
use eindir_core::{
    Bounds, boundary_anchored_low_discrepancy_points, halton_unit, low_discrepancy_points,
    shifted_low_discrepancy_points,
};
use ndarray::array;

fn main() {
    // Axis i of Halton point k is the radical inverse of k in the i-th prime.
    assert_eq!(halton_unit(1, 2), array![0.5, 1.0 / 3.0]);

    let bounds = Bounds::new(array![-5.12, -5.12], array![5.12, 5.12], 0.0);

    let starts = low_discrepancy_points(&bounds, 16, 1);
    assert_eq!(starts.shape(), &[16, 2]);
    assert!(starts.outer_iter().all(|x| bounds.contains(x)));
    println!("first start {}", starts.row(0));

    // The same seed gives the same replica; a different seed shifts the design.
    let a = shifted_low_discrepancy_points(&bounds, 16, 1, 3);
    let b = shifted_low_discrepancy_points(&bounds, 16, 1, 3);
    let c = shifted_low_discrepancy_points(&bounds, 16, 1, 4);
    assert_eq!(a, b);
    assert_ne!(a, c);

    // Four corners and the centre fit in the first five rows of a 2-D design.
    let anchored = boundary_anchored_low_discrepancy_points(&bounds, 16, 1);
    assert_eq!(anchored.row(0), array![-5.12, -5.12]);
    assert_eq!(anchored.row(3), array![5.12, 5.12]);
    assert_eq!(anchored.row(4), array![0.0, 0.0]);
    assert_eq!(anchored.row(5), starts.row(5));
    println!("anchored rows 0..5 hold the corners and the centre");
}
```

`cargo run --example low_discrepancy` runs it.
The Python and Rust functions give the same points for the same arguments.

### Choosing the arguments

- Use `skip` to continue a sequence across calls, for example to add points to a pilot design without repeating any.
- Use the shifted version when you need several independent designs of the same size, such as one per replica, or an error estimate across shifts.
- Use the anchored version when the optimum may sit on the boundary; a plain Halton design never hits a corner after point 0.
- In many dimensions, axes built on large primes can line up in pairs for small `n`; see the explanation page.

## GLE thermostat

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/tutorials/gle-thermostat.org

This tutorial builds the coloured-noise thermostat of the generalized Langevin equation (GLE), starts it at equilibrium and checks that the momenta keep their thermal variance.
The thermostat is Rust-only; Python has no binding for it.
[The GLE thermostat](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/explanation/gle.org) explains what it computes and why.

### The program

```rust
//! The coloured-noise GLE thermostat on its own: build the optimal-sampling
//! drift, start from the stationary distribution and check that the
//! physical momentum keeps its thermal variance. The GLE tutorial includes
//! this file; `cargo run --example gle_thermostat`.
use eindir_core::{GleThermostat, OPTIMAL_SAMPLING_NS, optimal_sampling_drift};
use ndarray::Array2;
use rand::SeedableRng;
use rand::rngs::StdRng;

fn main() {
    let mut rng = StdRng::seed_from_u64(0);

    // Flat sampling efficiency over [omega0, 100 omega0], in inverse time units.
    let omega0 = 0.2;
    let drift = optimal_sampling_drift(omega0);
    assert_eq!(drift.nrows(), OPTIMAL_SAMPLING_NS + 1);

    // Reduced units: kb = 1, so the momentum variance is the temperature.
    let (dt, temperature, kb) = (0.01, 1.0, 1.0);
    let gle = GleThermostat::canonical(&drift, dt, temperature, kb);

    // Row 0 is the mass-scaled physical momentum, rows 1..=ns the auxiliary ones.
    let covariance = Array2::<f64>::eye(gle.ns + 1) * temperature;
    let dim = 4;
    let mut state = gle.sample_stationary(&covariance, dim, kb, &mut rng);

    let steps = 20_000;
    let mut p2 = 0.0;
    for _ in 0..steps {
        gle.step(&mut state.view_mut(), &mut rng);
        p2 += state.row(0).mapv(|p| p * p).sum();
    }
    let mean_p2 = p2 / (steps * dim) as f64;
    println!("<p^2> = {mean_p2:.3} over {steps} steps, kB T = {temperature}");
    assert!((mean_p2 - temperature).abs() < 0.1);
}
```

`cargo run --example gle_thermostat` prints a value near 1:

```text
<p^2> = 0.970 over 20000 steps, kB T = 1
```

### What each call does

- `optimal_sampling_drift(omega0)` returns the drift matrix `A`, square of size `OPTIMAL_SAMPLING_NS + 1` (13).
  It is a fitted reference scaled by `omega0`, so the band it damps evenly is `[omega0, 100 omega0]`.
  Pick `omega0` near the slowest frequency you want to sample, in inverse units of `dt`.
- `GleThermostat::canonical(&drift, dt, temperature, kb)` precomputes the propagator `T = exp(-dt A)` and the noise factor `S` for one step.
  The fourth argument is Boltzmann's constant, not a mass; there is no mass argument because the state holds mass-scaled momenta.
- `sample_stationary(&c, dim, kb, &mut rng)` draws a state of shape `(ns + 1, dim)` from the stationary law `N(0, kb c)`.
  Pass the covariance the thermostat was built with, `temperature * I` for `canonical`.
- `step(&mut state.view_mut(), &mut rng)` applies `s <- T s + S xi` in place.
  Row 0 is the physical momentum of each coordinate and rows 1 to `ns` are the auxiliary momenta.

### In an integrator

The thermostat only updates momenta, and each call to `step` advances them by the `dt` it was built with.
Call it once per timestep between the force kicks of your integrator, or build it with `dt / 2` and call it before and after the kicks for a symmetric splitting.
The anneal GLE driver does this; [Using with anneal](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/howto/using-with-anneal.org) says where it plugs in.

## Surrogates

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/tutorials/surrogates.org

This tutorial fits an additive surrogate on a Halton pilot, draws proposals from it, and searches a function along one direction with a reduced objective.
The surrogates are Rust-only.
[Surrogates](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/explanation/surrogates.org) explains the models.

### The program

```rust
//! An additive Chebyshev surrogate fitted on a Halton pilot, its tempered
//! independence proposals, and a one-dimensional reduced objective. The
//! surrogates tutorial includes this file; `cargo run --example surrogates`.
use eindir_core::{
    AdditiveSurrogate, Bounds, Objective, Rastrigin, ReducedObjective, low_discrepancy_points,
};
use ndarray::{Array1, ArrayView1, array};
use rand::SeedableRng;
use rand::rngs::StdRng;

fn main() {
    let bounds = Bounds::new(array![-2.0, -2.0, -2.0], array![2.0, 2.0, 2.0], 0.0);
    let f = |x: ArrayView1<f64>| x[0] * x[0] + (2.0 * x[1]).sin() + 0.5 * x[2];

    // Fit c + sum_j g_j(x_j), each g_j a degree-8 Chebyshev series.
    let pilot = low_discrepancy_points(&bounds, 128, 1);
    let y: Array1<f64> = pilot.outer_iter().map(f).collect();
    let surrogate = AdditiveSurrogate::fit(pilot.view(), y.view(), bounds.clone(), 8);

    // The function is separable, so the fit is close on points it has not seen.
    let fresh = low_discrepancy_points(&bounds, 64, 1000);
    let worst = fresh
        .outer_iter()
        .map(|x| (surrogate.value(x) - f(x)).abs())
        .fold(0.0, f64::max);
    println!("worst error {worst:.2e} on 64 new points");
    assert!(worst < 1e-2);

    // Independence proposals from exp(-(f - f_min) / T), one coordinate at a time.
    let mut rng = StdRng::seed_from_u64(0);
    let proposals = surrogate.sample(5, 1.0, 256, &mut rng);
    assert!(proposals.outer_iter().all(|x| bounds.contains(x)));

    // Search 2-D Rastrigin along the diagonal x = (r, r) only.
    let reduced = ReducedObjective::new(
        Rastrigin::<2>::new(),
        array![0.0, 0.0],
        array![[1.0], [1.0]],
        Bounds::new(array![-5.12], array![5.12], 0.0),
    );
    assert_eq!(Objective::dim(&reduced), 1);
    println!(
        "reduced Rastrigin at r = 1: {}",
        reduced.eval(array![1.0].view())
    );
}
```

`cargo run --example surrogates` prints:

```text
worst error 5.24e-3 on 64 new points
reduced Rastrigin at r = 1: 2
```

### What each call does

- `AdditiveSurrogate::fit(x, y, bounds, degree)` fits `c + sum_j g_j(x_j)`, with each `g_j` a Chebyshev series up to degree `degree` in coordinate `j`.
  The rows of `x` are the pilot points and `y` their values; it needs more rows than `degree`.
  It runs 12 backfitting passes, refitting one coordinate at a time against the residual of the others; `fit_backfit` takes the number of passes.
- `value` and `gradient` evaluate the fit; the surrogate also implements `Objective` and `Gradient`, so any driver can use it in place of the true function.
- `sample(n, temperature, grid_m, &mut rng)` draws `n` points from `exp(-(f - f_min) / T)` of the fit, one coordinate at a time by inverse CDF on a grid of `grid_m` nodes.
  `temperature` is in the units of the fitted values.
  These are proposals: a sampler should accept or reject them with the true objective.
- `ReducedObjective::new(inner, origin, basis, bounds)` evaluates `inner` at `origin + basis r`, where `r` lives in the box `bounds` of dimension `basis.ncols()`.
  Here the basis is the diagonal, so `r = 1` is the point `(1, 1)`.
- `ChebyshevSurrogate::new(bounds, terms, coeffs)` is a total-degree Chebyshev polynomial with given coefficients, for use on the reduced box; eindir does not fit it.

Write `Objective::dim(&reduced)` when the type also implements `Gradient`, since `reduced.dim()` is then ambiguous.

## Installation

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/howto/install.org

### Python from PyPI

```bash
pip install eindir
```

The wheel is abi3 and needs Python 3.10 or newer.
The extras are `plotter` (matplotlib and cmcrameri) and `testing` (array-api-strict, pytest and pytest-cov), as in `pip install "eindir[plotter]"`.
There is no `all` extra.

The newest release on PyPI is 0.5.1, which predates the bounds checks, the docstrings and several of the functions on these pages.
Run `pip index versions eindir` to see what is released, and build from source for the main branch.

### Rust from crates.io

```toml
[dependencies]
eindir-core = "0.6"
```

The crate needs Rust 1.88 or newer (edition 2024).
Its optional features are `autodiff` (forward-mode gradients), `capi` (the C ABI), `python` and `py-objective` (the Python extension).
`cargo info eindir-core` shows the newest release; for the main branch use a git dependency:

```toml
[dependencies]
eindir-core = { git = "https://github.com/HaoZeke/eindir" }
```

### Python from source

In a virtual environment with Rust 1.88 or newer:

```bash
python -m pip install "maturin>=1.5,<2" numpy
maturin develop --features python
python -c "import eindir; print(eindir._core.__version__)"
```

### C and C++ from source

The C library, its header `eindir-core.h` and `eindir-core.pc` come from cargo-c 0.10.17 or newer:

```bash
cargo install cargo-c
cargo cinstall --release --prefix="$HOME/.local" --libdir=lib
```

The header includes `dlpack/dlpack.h` and needs the DLPack 1.0 headers; distribution packages may ship an older version without `DLManagedTensorVersioned`.
Link against the installed prefix, not `target/`: the library's soname names a file that only `cinstall` creates.
[Bindings](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/bindings.org) has the Meson and CMake snippets.

### Pixi

[pixi](https://pixi.sh) supplies Rust, Python, maturin and the documentation tools in three environments:

```bash
pixi install
pixi run -e python python-test   # build the extension and run pytest
pixi run -e docs docbld          # build this manual into docs/build
```

## Gradients

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/howto/gradients.org

Gradient-based drivers such as the GLE Langevin driver and local polish in anneal take a type that implements `Gradient<f64>`, usually through `DifferentiableObjective<f64>`.
This page shows how to provide one from Rust, from Python and from C.

### Rust

There are four routes, from most to least work:

- Implement `Gradient<f64>` on the objective type and add `impl DifferentiableObjective<f64> for T {}`.
  There is no blanket impl, so the empty impl is required; override `value_and_gradient` when the value and gradient share work.
- Wrap a gradient closure in `AnalyticGradient::new(dim, grad_fn)`.
- Write the function once over dual numbers and wrap it in `ForwardAd` (feature `autodiff`; the field uses the `num-dual` crate).
  `ForwardAd` implements `Objective`, `Gradient` and `DifferentiableObjective`, with exact partial derivatives from one evaluation.
- Wrap any objective in `FiniteDiffGradient::new(obj)`.
  It uses central differences with an absolute step `h = 1e-5` (`with_step` changes it), so one gradient costs `2 * dim` evaluations, and the stencil can step up to `h` outside the bounds.
  It implements `Gradient` only.

```rust
//! Three ways to give an objective a gradient: implement `Gradient` by hand
//! with a fused value and gradient, pair a closure with `AnalyticGradient`,
//! or difference the objective with `FiniteDiffGradient`. The gradients
//! how-to includes this file; `cargo run --example gradients`.
use eindir_core::{
    AnalyticGradient, Bounds, DifferentiableObjective, FiniteDiffGradient, Gradient, Objective,
};
use ndarray::{Array1, ArrayView1, array};

/// `f(x) = sum_i exp(x_i)`, whose gradient reuses the exponentials.
struct ExpSum {
    bounds: Bounds<f64>,
}

impl Objective<f64> for ExpSum {
    fn dim(&self) -> usize {
        self.bounds.dims
    }
    fn bounds(&self) -> &Bounds<f64> {
        &self.bounds
    }
    fn eval(&self, x: ArrayView1<f64>) -> f64 {
        x.mapv(f64::exp).sum()
    }
}

impl Gradient<f64> for ExpSum {
    fn dim(&self) -> usize {
        self.bounds.dims
    }
    fn grad(&self, x: ArrayView1<f64>) -> Array1<f64> {
        x.mapv(f64::exp)
    }
}

// No blanket impl exists, so opt in; override to fuse the two passes.
impl DifferentiableObjective<f64> for ExpSum {
    fn value_and_gradient(&self, x: ArrayView1<f64>) -> (f64, Array1<f64>) {
        let e = x.mapv(f64::exp);
        (e.sum(), e)
    }
}

fn main() {
    let bounds = Bounds::new(array![-1.0, -1.0], array![1.0, 1.0], 0.0);
    let f = ExpSum {
        bounds: bounds.clone(),
    };
    let x = array![0.0, 0.5];

    // Objective::dim, since f.dim() would be ambiguous here.
    assert_eq!(Objective::dim(&f), 2);
    let (value, g) = f.value_and_gradient(x.view());
    println!("f = {value:.6}, grad = {g}");

    let closure = AnalyticGradient::new(2, |x: ArrayView1<f64>| x.mapv(f64::exp));
    assert_eq!(closure.grad(x.view()), g);

    // Central differences: 2 * dim evaluations, error of order h^2.
    let fd = FiniteDiffGradient::new(ExpSum { bounds });
    let err = (&fd.grad(x.view()) - &g).mapv(f64::abs).sum();
    println!("finite-difference error {err:.1e}");
    assert!(err < 1e-8);
}
```

On a type that implements both `Objective` and `Gradient`, `x.dim()` is ambiguous (error E0034); write `Objective::dim(&x)`.

Nothing in eindir adds a finite-difference gradient for you: a driver that needs a gradient will not compile against an objective without one.

### Python

Pass `grad_fn` to `PyObjective`:

```python
import numpy as np
from eindir import _core

bounds = _core.Bounds(np.full(2, -1.0), np.full(2, 1.0))
obj = _core.PyObjective(
    lambda x: float(np.sum(np.exp(x))),
    bounds,
    grad_fn=lambda x: np.exp(x),
)
print(obj.grad(np.array([0.0, 0.5])))
```

Without `grad_fn`, `obj.grad` raises `ValueError`; Python has no finite-difference fallback.
If you have no gradient, difference the function yourself in `grad_fn`.

### C

Set `grad_fn` in `eindir_objective_new` and advertise `EINDIR_FEATURE_GRADIENT` in the descriptor.
A NULL `grad_fn` makes `EindirObjectiveWrapper::grad` return zeros.
[Objectives through the C ABI](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/howto/c-objective.org) has a complete example.

## Objectives through the C ABI

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/howto/c-objective.org

This page writes an objective in C, checks that the library it runs against is compatible, and hands the objective to Rust code.
[The C ABI](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/explanation/c-abi.org) explains the design and [C API](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/reference/c-api.org) lists every function.

### Install the library and the DLPack headers

```bash
cargo install cargo-c
cargo cinstall --release --prefix="$HOME/.local" --libdir=lib
```

`eindir-core.h` includes `dlpack/dlpack.h`, which must be DLPack 1.0 or newer.
Ubuntu's `libdlpack-dev` is 0.6 and lacks `DLManagedTensorVersioned`, so fetch the headers of the [v1.0 release](https://github.com/dmlc/dlpack/releases/tag/v1.0) instead.

Build and link against the installed prefix:

```bash
export PKG_CONFIG_PATH="$HOME/.local/lib/pkgconfig"
cc -std=c99 -Wall -I/path/to/dlpack/include objective_demo.c \
  $(pkg-config --cflags --libs eindir-core) -Wl,-rpath,"$HOME/.local/lib" -o objective_demo
```

Linking against `target/` after `cargo cbuild` gives a program that does not start, because the soname, for example `libeindir_core.so.0.8`, names a file only `cinstall` creates.

### Check the library at startup

Compare the library's ABI stamp with the one your code was built against before using any handle:

```c
const eindir_abi_stamp_t stamp = eindir_core_abi_stamp();
if (!eindir_core_abi_compatible(&stamp) || stamp.dlpack_major != DLPACK_MAJOR_VERSION) {
    /* refuse to run */
}
```

`eindir_core_abi_compatible` returns 1 when the major ABI version, the handle layout and size, and the DLPack major version are equal and the library's minor versions and feature bits are at least those of the stamp.
To use the fallible handle, also check `stamp.features & EINDIR_ABI_FEATURE_TRY_CALLBACKS`.

### Write the callbacks

A value callback has the type `EindirEvalFn` and a gradient callback `EindirGradFn`:

```c
enum eindir_status_t eval(void *user_data, const struct DLManagedTensorVersioned *x,
                          double *value_out);
enum eindir_status_t grad(void *user_data, const struct DLManagedTensorVersioned *x,
                          struct DLManagedTensorVersioned *grad_out);
```

Return `EINDIR_SUCCESS` after writing the result, or `EINDIR_INVALID_PARAMETER` or `EINDIR_INTERNAL_ERROR`.
eindir does not check the tensors it passes on from a caller, so a callback that can receive tensors from C code should check `ndim`, `shape`, `dtype`, the device and `strides` itself, as `is_f64_vector` does in the program below.
Tensors built by the Rust wrapper are always contiguous 1-D CPU float64 vectors of length `dim`.

### Create a handle

`eindir_objective_new(dim, low, high, eval_fn, grad_fn, user_data, free_fn)` copies the bounds and returns a handle, or NULL with a message in `eindir_last_error()`.
Pass NULL for `grad_fn` when there is no gradient.
`eindir_objective_free` calls `free_fn(user_data)` when both are non-NULL, then frees the handle.

To carry units and signs, embed `eindir_objective_t` as the first member of your own struct, fill its fields, and point `descriptor` at a static `eindir_objective_descriptor_t`.
A consumer then checks it with `eindir_objective_descriptor_compatible(actual, required)`, where empty fields of `required` accept anything, except `schema_id`, which must be set and equal.
Free an embedded handle with your own destructor, never with `eindir_objective_free`.

### Report failures with a message

The fallible handle `eindir_try_objective_t` takes callbacks that return an `int32_t` status and write a message into a buffer of `EINDIR_TRY_MESSAGE_CAP` (256) bytes:

```c
int32_t try_eval(void *user_data, const struct DLManagedTensorVersioned *x,
                 double *value_out, char *message_out, uintptr_t message_cap);
```

Status 0 is success, 1 and 2 mean invalid parameter and internal error, and any other value is yours.
`eindir_try_objective_eval` returns the status and copies the message into the caller's buffer and into `eindir_last_error()`.
A message in plain UTF-8 without backslashes arrives unchanged; other bytes are escaped as the [C API reference](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/reference/c-api.org) describes.

### The complete program

This program does all of the above and checks each result.
CI builds and runs it, under valgrind when it is available.

```c
/* A C objective through the eindir C ABI: DLPack tensors for bounds and
 * points, value and gradient callbacks, error reporting, an embedded
 * handle with a semantic descriptor, and cleanup. Exits non-zero on the
 * first check that fails. */
#include <dlpack/dlpack.h>
#include <eindir-core.h>

#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>

#define DIM 3

#define CHECK(cond, what)                                                   \
    do {                                                                    \
        if (!(cond)) {                                                      \
            fprintf(stderr, "FAIL: %s (eindir_last_error: %s)\n", (what),   \
                    eindir_last_error());                                   \
            return 1;                                                       \
        }                                                                   \
    } while (0)

/* A borrowed, contiguous, one-dimensional float64 CPU tensor over data. */
static struct DLManagedTensorVersioned vector(double *data, int64_t *shape) {
    struct DLManagedTensorVersioned t;
    memset(&t, 0, sizeof t);
    t.version.major = DLPACK_MAJOR_VERSION;
    t.version.minor = DLPACK_MINOR_VERSION;
    t.dl_tensor.data = data;
    t.dl_tensor.device.device_type = kDLCPU;
    t.dl_tensor.ndim = 1;
    t.dl_tensor.dtype.code = kDLFloat;
    t.dl_tensor.dtype.bits = 64;
    t.dl_tensor.dtype.lanes = 1;
    t.dl_tensor.shape = shape;
    return t;
}

/* eindir hands x to the callbacks unchecked, so they check it. */
static int is_f64_vector(const struct DLManagedTensorVersioned *t, int64_t n) {
    const DLTensor *x = &t->dl_tensor;
    return x->data != NULL && x->ndim == 1 && x->shape[0] == n &&
           x->dtype.code == kDLFloat && x->dtype.bits == 64 &&
           x->dtype.lanes == 1 && x->device.device_type == kDLCPU &&
           (x->strides == NULL || x->strides[0] == 1);
}

static double *elements(const struct DLManagedTensorVersioned *t) {
    return (double *)((char *)t->dl_tensor.data + t->dl_tensor.byte_offset);
}

/* f(x) = sum_i (x_i - centre_i)^2, counting evaluations. */
struct sphere {
    double centre[DIM];
    unsigned evals;
    int *freed;
};

static enum eindir_status_t sphere_eval(void *user_data,
                                        const struct DLManagedTensorVersioned *x,
                                        double *value_out) {
    struct sphere *s = user_data;
    const double *xs;
    double sum = 0.0;
    int i;
    if (!is_f64_vector(x, DIM)) {
        return EINDIR_INVALID_PARAMETER;
    }
    xs = elements(x);
    for (i = 0; i < DIM; ++i) {
        sum += (xs[i] - s->centre[i]) * (xs[i] - s->centre[i]);
    }
    s->evals++;
    *value_out = sum;
    return EINDIR_SUCCESS;
}

static enum eindir_status_t sphere_grad(void *user_data,
                                        const struct DLManagedTensorVersioned *x,
                                        struct DLManagedTensorVersioned *grad_out) {
    struct sphere *s = user_data;
    const double *xs;
    double *g;
    int i;
    if (!is_f64_vector(x, DIM) || !is_f64_vector(grad_out, DIM)) {
        return EINDIR_INVALID_PARAMETER;
    }
    xs = elements(x);
    g = elements(grad_out);
    for (i = 0; i < DIM; ++i) {
        g[i] = 2.0 * (xs[i] - s->centre[i]);
    }
    return EINDIR_SUCCESS;
}

#define SPHERE_REFUSED 7

/* A fallible callback: a status and a message. Refuses x[0] above 10. */
static int32_t try_sphere_eval(void *user_data,
                               const struct DLManagedTensorVersioned *x,
                               double *value_out, char *message_out,
                               uintptr_t message_cap) {
    const double *xs;
    double sum = 0.0;
    int i;
    (void)user_data;
    if (!is_f64_vector(x, DIM)) {
        snprintf(message_out, message_cap, "x is not a float64 vector of length %d",
                 DIM);
        return EINDIR_TRY_INVALID_PARAMETER;
    }
    xs = elements(x);
    if (xs[0] > 10.0) {
        snprintf(message_out, message_cap, "geometry refused: x[0] = %g", xs[0]);
        return SPHERE_REFUSED;
    }
    for (i = 0; i < DIM; ++i) {
        sum += xs[i] * xs[i];
    }
    *value_out = sum;
    return EINDIR_TRY_SUCCESS;
}

static void free_sphere(void *user_data) {
    struct sphere *s = user_data;
    *s->freed = 1;
    free(s);
}

/* An objective embedded as the first member of a producer's own struct. */
struct producer {
    eindir_objective_t base;
    double low[DIM];
    double high[DIM];
    struct sphere sphere;
};

static const eindir_objective_descriptor_t produced = {
    .schema_id = "eindir.objective-descriptor.v1",
    .producer_id = "example.sphere",
    .length_unit = "angstrom",
    .energy_unit = "eV",
    .energy_sign = 1,
    .gradient_sign = 1,
    .operations =
        EINDIR_OBJECTIVE_OPERATION_ENERGY | EINDIR_OBJECTIVE_OPERATION_FORCES,
    .tensor_device_type = EINDIR_TENSOR_DEVICE_CPU,
    .tensor_dtype_code = EINDIR_TENSOR_DTYPE_FLOAT,
    .tensor_dtype_bits = 64,
    .tensor_dtype_lanes = 1,
    .tensor_layout = EINDIR_TENSOR_LAYOUT_CONTIGUOUS,
    .callback_lifetime = EINDIR_CALLBACK_LIFETIME_BORROWED_SYNC,
};

int main(void) {
    const eindir_abi_stamp_t stamp = eindir_core_abi_stamp();
    double low[DIM] = {-5.0, -5.0, -5.0};
    double high[DIM] = {5.0, 5.0, 5.0};
    double x[DIM] = {0.0, 0.0, 0.0};
    double g[DIM] = {0.0, 0.0, 0.0};
    double back[DIM] = {0.0, 0.0, 0.0};
    double pair[2] = {0.0, 0.0};
    double far[DIM] = {11.0, 0.0, 0.0};
    int64_t shape[1] = {DIM};
    int64_t pair_shape[1] = {2};
    struct DLManagedTensorVersioned low_t = vector(low, shape);
    struct DLManagedTensorVersioned high_t = vector(high, shape);
    struct DLManagedTensorVersioned x_t = vector(x, shape);
    struct DLManagedTensorVersioned g_t = vector(g, shape);
    struct DLManagedTensorVersioned back_t = vector(back, shape);
    struct DLManagedTensorVersioned pair_t = vector(pair, pair_shape);
    struct DLManagedTensorVersioned far_t = vector(far, shape);
    struct sphere plain_ctx = {{1.0, 2.0, 3.0}, 0, NULL};
    struct sphere *ctx;
    eindir_objective_t *obj;
    eindir_objective_t *plain;
    eindir_try_objective_t *tried;
    eindir_objective_descriptor_t required;
    struct producer p;
    char message[256];
    double f = 0.0;
    int32_t status;
    int freed = 0;
    int i;

    CHECK(strcmp(eindir_core_abi_family(), "eindir.objective") == 0, "ABI family");
    CHECK(eindir_core_abi_compatible(&stamp), "ABI stamp");
    CHECK(stamp.dlpack_major == DLPACK_MAJOR_VERSION, "DLPack major version");
    CHECK(stamp.features & EINDIR_ABI_FEATURE_GRADIENT, "gradient feature bit");
    printf("eindir-core %s: ABI %u.%u, objective layout %u, DLPack %u.%u\n",
           eindir_core_version(), stamp.abi_major, stamp.abi_minor,
           stamp.objective_layout, stamp.dlpack_major, stamp.dlpack_minor);

    ctx = malloc(sizeof *ctx);
    CHECK(ctx != NULL, "malloc");
    *ctx = plain_ctx;
    ctx->freed = &freed;
    obj = eindir_objective_new(DIM, &low_t, &high_t, sphere_eval, sphere_grad,
                               ctx, free_sphere);
    CHECK(obj != NULL, "eindir_objective_new");
    CHECK(eindir_objective_dim(obj) == DIM, "eindir_objective_dim");
    CHECK(eindir_objective_has_grad(obj) == 1, "eindir_objective_has_grad");
    CHECK(eindir_objective_descriptor(obj) == NULL,
          "handles from eindir_objective_new carry no descriptor");
    low[0] = -1.0;
    CHECK(eindir_objective_bounds_low(obj, &back_t) == EINDIR_SUCCESS &&
              back[0] == -5.0,
          "eindir_objective_new copied the bounds");

    CHECK(eindir_objective_eval(obj, &x_t, &f) == EINDIR_SUCCESS && f == 14.0,
          "eindir_objective_eval");
    CHECK(eindir_objective_grad(obj, &x_t, &g_t) == EINDIR_SUCCESS &&
              g[0] == -2.0 && g[1] == -4.0 && g[2] == -6.0,
          "eindir_objective_grad");
    printf("f(0) = %g, grad f(0) = [%g, %g, %g], %u evaluation(s)\n", f, g[0],
           g[1], g[2], ctx->evals);

    CHECK(eindir_objective_new(DIM, &pair_t, &high_t, sphere_eval, NULL, NULL,
                               NULL) == NULL,
          "bounds of the wrong length are refused");
    printf("wrong bounds length: %s\n", eindir_last_error());
    CHECK(eindir_objective_eval(NULL, &x_t, &f) == EINDIR_INVALID_PARAMETER,
          "NULL objective");
    printf("NULL objective: %s\n", eindir_last_error());
    snprintf(message, sizeof message, "%s", eindir_last_error());
    CHECK(eindir_objective_eval(obj, &pair_t, &f) == EINDIR_INVALID_PARAMETER,
          "the callback refuses a 2-vector");
    CHECK(strcmp(eindir_last_error(), message) == 0,
          "a failing callback leaves the last error in place");

    plain = eindir_objective_new(DIM, &low_t, &high_t, sphere_eval, NULL,
                                 &plain_ctx, NULL);
    CHECK(plain != NULL && eindir_objective_has_grad(plain) == 0,
          "an objective without a gradient callback");
    CHECK(eindir_objective_grad(plain, &x_t, &g_t) == EINDIR_INVALID_PARAMETER,
          "grad without a gradient callback");
    printf("gradient without a callback: %s\n", eindir_last_error());
    snprintf(message, sizeof message, "%s", eindir_last_error());
    CHECK(eindir_objective_eval(plain, &x_t, &f) == EINDIR_SUCCESS,
          "eval after an error");
    CHECK(strcmp(eindir_last_error(), message) == 0,
          "a success leaves the last error in place");
    eindir_objective_free(plain);

    for (i = 0; i < DIM; ++i) {
        p.low[i] = -5.0;
        p.high[i] = 5.0;
    }
    p.sphere = plain_ctx;
    p.base.dim = DIM;
    p.base.low = p.low;
    p.base.high = p.high;
    p.base.eval_fn = sphere_eval;
    p.base.grad_fn = sphere_grad;
    p.base.user_data = &p.sphere;
    p.base.free_fn = NULL;
    p.base.descriptor = &produced;
    CHECK(eindir_objective_eval(&p.base, &x_t, &f) == EINDIR_SUCCESS && f == 14.0,
          "eval through an embedded handle");
    CHECK(eindir_objective_descriptor(&p.base) == &produced,
          "an embedded handle returns its descriptor");

    memset(&required, 0, sizeof required);
    required.schema_id = produced.schema_id;
    required.operations = EINDIR_OBJECTIVE_OPERATION_ENERGY;
    required.tensor_dtype_bits = 64;
    CHECK(eindir_objective_descriptor_compatible(&produced, &required) == 1,
          "zero and empty fields are wildcards");
    required.energy_unit = "hartree";
    CHECK(eindir_objective_descriptor_compatible(&produced, &required) == 0,
          "a unit mismatch is refused");
    printf("energy unit mismatch: %s\n", eindir_last_error());
    required.energy_unit = "";
    required.schema_id = "";
    CHECK(eindir_objective_descriptor_compatible(&produced, &required) == 0,
          "schema_id is never a wildcard");

    tried = eindir_try_objective_new(DIM, &low_t, &high_t, try_sphere_eval, NULL,
                                     NULL, NULL);
    CHECK(tried != NULL && eindir_try_objective_has_grad(tried) == 0,
          "eindir_try_objective_new");
    CHECK(stamp.features & EINDIR_ABI_FEATURE_TRY_CALLBACKS,
          "fallible callback feature bit");
    status = eindir_try_objective_eval(tried, &x_t, &f, message, sizeof message);
    CHECK(status == EINDIR_TRY_SUCCESS && f == 0.0 && message[0] == '\0',
          "a fallible callback that succeeds");
    status = eindir_try_objective_eval(tried, &far_t, &f, message, sizeof message);
    CHECK(status == SPHERE_REFUSED, "the callback's own status comes back");
    CHECK(strcmp(eindir_last_error(), message) == 0,
          "the message is also the last error");
    printf("fallible callback: status %d, message \"%s\"\n", (int)status, message);
    status = eindir_try_objective_eval(tried, &pair_t, &f, NULL, 0);
    CHECK(status == EINDIR_TRY_INVALID_PARAMETER,
          "a NULL message buffer is allowed");
    eindir_try_objective_free(tried);

    eindir_objective_free(obj);
    CHECK(freed == 1, "eindir_objective_free called free_fn");
    eindir_objective_free(NULL);
    printf("all checks passed\n");
    return 0;
}
```

Its output:

```text
eindir-core 0.8.0: ABI 1.2, objective layout 3, DLPack 1.0
f(0) = 14, grad f(0) = [-2, -4, -6], 1 evaluation(s)
wrong bounds length: eindir_objective_new: bounds_low length 2 != dim 3
NULL objective: eindir_objective_eval: obj is NULL
gradient without a callback: eindir_objective_grad: no gradient callback
energy unit mismatch: eindir objective semantic descriptor mismatch
fallible callback: status 7, message "geometry refused: x[0] = 11"
all checks passed
```

### Use the objective from Rust

A Rust driver that receives a handle pointer wraps it:

- `EindirObjectiveWrapper::new(&*ptr)` implements `Objective<f64>`, `Gradient<f64>` and `DifferentiableObjective<f64>`.
  A failing value callback becomes NaN; a missing gradient callback gives zeros and the status of the gradient callback is ignored.
- `EindirTryObjectiveWrapper::new(&*ptr)` implements the fallible traits with `Error = CallbackError`, which holds the status and the message.
  A missing gradient callback is an error with status 1.

Both constructors are `unsafe`: `low` and `high` must point to `dim` doubles, and they panic when `low[i] > high[i]`.
The wrappers copy the bounds once, with slack 0.

### C++

The C header compiles as C++.
`include/eindir-core.hpp` adds only `eindir::version()`; there are no C++ classes for the handles.
`skills/eindir-c-abi/assets/raii_demo.cpp` shows a `std::unique_ptr` with a custom deleter.

## Objectives that can fail

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/howto/fallible.org

This page writes an objective whose evaluation returns an error, passes the error through a generic driver unchanged, and turns it back into a NaN for code that expects the infallible traits.
[Fallible objectives](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/explanation/fallible-objectives.org) explains the traits.

### Steps

1. Pick an error type.
   Any type works; eindir puts no bound on it.
2. Write the objective as a `TryOracle::new(bounds, f)`, where `f` returns `Result<(value, gradient), E>`, or implement `TryObjective` and `TryGradient` on your own type with the same `E` for `Error` and `GradError`.
   Do not implement `TryObjective` on a type that implements `Objective`; it already has one.
3. Write the driver generic over `O: TryDifferentiableObjective<f64>` and return `O::Error` with `?`.
   Infallible objectives such as `Rastrigin` pass through the same driver with `Error = Infallible`.
4. Where code needs the infallible traits, wrap the objective in `NanOnError::new(inner, sink)`, which returns NaN and hands each error to `sink`, or in `PanicOnError::new(inner)` for tests.

### The program

```rust
//! An objective whose evaluation can fail: the error reaches a generic
//! driver unchanged, and an infallible objective passes through the same
//! driver. The fallible-objective how-to includes this file;
//! `cargo run --example fallible_objective`.
use eindir_core::{
    Bounds, NanOnError, Objective, Rastrigin, TryDifferentiableObjective, TryOracle,
};
use ndarray::{Array1, ArrayView1, array};

#[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
enum EngineError {
    Refused { x0: f64 },
}

/// One steepest-descent step that returns the objective's own error.
fn descend<O>(obj: &O, x: &mut Array1<f64>, step: f64) -> Result<f64, O::Error>
where
    O: TryDifferentiableObjective<f64>,
{
    let (_, g) = obj.try_value_and_gradient(x.view())?;
    *x = &*x - &(g * step);
    let (value, _) = obj.try_value_and_gradient(x.view())?;
    Ok(value)
}

fn main() {
    let bounds = Bounds::new(array![-5.0, -5.0], array![5.0, 5.0], 0.0);
    let engine = TryOracle::new(bounds, |x: ArrayView1<f64>| {
        if x[0] > 4.0 {
            return Err(EngineError::Refused { x0: x[0] });
        }
        Ok((x.dot(&x), &x * 2.0))
    });

    let mut x = array![1.0, 1.0];
    assert_eq!(descend(&engine, &mut x, 0.25), Ok(0.5));

    let mut far = array![4.5, 0.0];
    assert_eq!(
        descend(&engine, &mut far, 0.25),
        Err(EngineError::Refused { x0: 4.5 })
    );

    // An infallible objective is a fallible one with Error = Infallible.
    let mut y = array![0.1, 0.0];
    let value = descend(&Rastrigin::<2>::new(), &mut y, 0.001).unwrap_or_else(|e| match e {});
    println!("Rastrigin after one step: {value:.4}");

    // Back to the infallible traits, keeping each error in a log.
    let log = std::sync::Mutex::new(Vec::new());
    let plain = NanOnError::new(engine, |e| log.lock().unwrap().push(e));
    assert!(plain.eval(array![4.5, 0.0].view()).is_nan());
    println!("logged: {:?}", log.lock().unwrap());
}
```

`cargo run --example fallible_objective` prints:

```text
Rastrigin after one step: 0.7740
logged: [Refused { x0: 4.5 }]
```

### From C

A C objective that wants to say why it failed uses `eindir_try_objective_t` and returns a status with a message; in Rust, `EindirTryObjectiveWrapper` turns those into a `CallbackError { code, message }`.
See [Objectives through the C ABI](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/howto/c-objective.org).

## Using with anneal

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/howto/using-with-anneal.org

[anneal](https://github.com/HaoZeke/anneal) builds simulated annealing and related samplers from five components: the objective (Obj), the cooling schedule (Cool), the neighbourhood (Neigh), the move (Move) and the acceptance rule (Accept).
eindir supplies the objective and several of the pieces the other components use.
This page says which eindir item goes where; the anneal documentation covers the drivers themselves.

### Objective

Every anneal driver takes an `eindir_core::Objective<f64>`.
Gradient-based drivers, such as the GLE Langevin driver and local polish, take a type that also implements `Gradient<f64>`; [Gradients](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/howto/gradients.org) shows how to provide one.
From Python, wrap a function with `eindir._core.PyObjective`.

### Start points and pilot designs

- The Bayesian pilot draws its design from `halton_unit`.
- Local polish draws its starts from `shifted_low_discrepancy_points` and `boundary_anchored_low_discrepancy_points`.

Use the same functions to seed your own chains, so that a change of driver does not also change the starts.
[Low-discrepancy points](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/tutorials/low-discrepancy.org) shows the calls.

### GLE moves

The GLE Langevin driver builds its thermostat from `optimal_sampling_drift` and `GleThermostat`.
One drift matrix serves every timestep and temperature, because the drift sets how fast the momenta decorrelate and the covariance alone sets the temperature.
[The GLE thermostat](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/explanation/gle.org) explains why.

### Surrogates

The additive independence driver fits an `AdditiveSurrogate` and draws proposals from it with `sample`, then accepts or rejects them with the true objective.
Because the surrogate implements `Objective`, the same fitted object can also stand in for the objective where a cheap value is enough.

## FAQ

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/howto/faq.org

### Why does an example from an older page fail with ImportError?

Earlier versions of this manual imported `Bounds`, `Objective`, `GleThermostat` and `AdditiveSurrogate` from `eindir`, and none of them exist there.
`Bounds` and `PyObjective` are in `eindir._core`, and the GLE thermostat, the surrogates, the gradient adapters and the test-function types are Rust-only.
[Python API](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/reference/api-primitives.org) lists what Python has.

### How do I give a driver a gradient?

In Rust, implement `Gradient<f64>` and add `impl DifferentiableObjective<f64> for T {}`, or use `AnalyticGradient`, `ForwardAd` or `FiniteDiffGradient`.
In Python, pass `grad_fn` to `PyObjective`; there is no finite-difference fallback.
[Gradients](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/howto/gradients.org) has the details.

### Can I use eindir without anneal?

Yes.
The objective traits, the point sets, the GLE thermostat and the surrogates depend on nothing in anneal.

### Why does Python raise TypeError for my list?

`eindir._core` takes contiguous float64 NumPy arrays only, so lists, integer arrays and strided views raise `TypeError`.
Convert with `np.ascontiguousarray(x, dtype=np.float64)`.
`eindir.low_discrepancy_points` converts for you.

### Why does `except Exception` not catch an error from `_core`?

A Rust panic reaches Python as `pyo3_runtime.PanicException`, which derives from `BaseException`.
`_core.Bounds` panics when `low > high`, `Bounds.clip` when the point has the wrong length, and a `PyObjective` when called from another thread.

### Can I use eindir from C or C++?

Yes, through `libeindir_core` and `eindir-core.h`, built with cargo-c.
The header compiles as C++; `eindir-core.hpp` adds only `eindir::version()`.
See [Objectives through the C ABI](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/howto/c-objective.org) and [Bindings](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/bindings.org).

### What licence is eindir under?

MIT; see `LICENSE` in the repository.

### How do I cite eindir?

Cite the software record on Zenodo.
The concept DOI [10.5281/zenodo.10672737](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10672737) always resolves to the newest archived version; the record for v0.5.2 is [10.5281/zenodo.21428233](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21428233).

```bibtex
@software{goswami_eindir,
  author    = {Goswami, Rohit},
  title     = {{eindir}},
  publisher = {Zenodo},
  doi       = {10.5281/zenodo.10672737},
  url       = {https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10672737}
}
```

When you use eindir through anneal, also cite the anneal reproducibility harness, [10.5281/zenodo.20672621](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20672621).
Cite the methods behind the primitives as listed on the [GLE](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/explanation/gle.org), [low-discrepancy](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/explanation/low-discrepancy.org) and [surrogate](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/explanation/surrogates.org) pages.

## The primitives

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/explanation/primitives.org

eindir is a small set of pieces that optimisers and samplers share.
Each piece is a trait or a plain function, so a driver can combine them without depending on any other driver.

### Objectives and bounds

`Objective<T>` is a function from a box in R^D to a number: `dim`, `bounds` and `eval`, with `eval_batch` and `global_min` as provided methods.
`Bounds<T>` is the box, with a slack that `contains` allows outside it, `clip` and a random `mkpoint`.
Everything else either consumes an objective (drivers, point sets that feed them) or produces one (surrogates, reduced objectives, wrappers of Python and C functions).

The trait cannot fail and has no gradient.
Gradients come from a separate trait, `Gradient<T>`, so that an objective without one is still a complete objective, and `DifferentiableObjective<T>` joins the two with a fused `value_and_gradient`.
Failure comes from a separate family, `TryObjective` and its relatives, so that an infallible objective pays nothing for it; see [Fallible objectives](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/explanation/fallible-objectives.org).

`eval_batch_parallel` evaluates rows with rayon from `EVAL_BATCH_PARALLEL_MIN` rows up.
It needs `Sync` objectives, which every `Objective` is, and keeps the row order.

### Point sets

Halton designs are deterministic and well spread; they seed starts, pilots and surrogate fits.
See [Low-discrepancy point sets](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/explanation/low-discrepancy.org).

### The GLE thermostat

A momentum thermostat with coloured noise that samples a band of frequencies evenly, for gradient-based samplers.
See [The GLE thermostat](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/explanation/gle.org).

### Surrogates

Cheap models fitted on a pilot design that implement `Objective` themselves.
See [Surrogates](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/explanation/surrogates.org).

### Bindings

The Python extension wraps a Python function as `PyObjective` and exposes the point sets.
The C ABI wraps a C function as `eindir_objective_t`, which Rust code sees as an `Objective` through `EindirObjectiveWrapper`.
See [The C ABI](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/explanation/c-abi.org) and [Python API](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/reference/api-primitives.org).

## Low-discrepancy point sets

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/explanation/low-discrepancy.org

### Why not random points

Independent uniform points cluster and leave gaps by chance.
A low-discrepancy sequence places each new point where the earlier ones left room, so every box-shaped region holds close to its share of the points.
For smooth integrands this gives quasi-Monte Carlo errors that shrink faster with `n` than the `1/sqrt(n)` of Monte Carlo, and for optimisation and fitting it gives starts and pilot designs that cover the box evenly.
The points are also deterministic: the same arguments give the same design in Rust and in Python, so a benchmark that changes the optimiser does not change its starts as well.

### The Halton sequence

`radical_inverse(k, b)` writes `k` in base `b` and mirrors the digits about the radix point: in base 2, `k = 6 = 110` becomes `0.011 = 0.375`.
Halton point `k` in `d` dimensions takes the radical inverse of `k` in the first `d` primes, one prime per axis [1]; `halton_unit(k, d)` returns it.
`halton_points(bounds, n, skip)` scales points `skip` to `skip + n - 1` into the box, and `low_discrepancy_points` is the same function.
Point 0 is the corner `low`, so `skip = 1` is the usual choice.

eindir grows its prime table on demand, so designs with thousands of axes cost one table extension instead of a search per axis.
Rows are computed in parallel from 64 rows up, with the same result as the serial path.

In many dimensions the Halton sequence has a known weakness: the axes built on two large primes advance almost in step for the first points, so their projection shows lines instead of an even cover.
Skipping more of the sequence, or shifting it, reduces the effect for small `n`.

### Shifted designs

`shifted_low_discrepancy_points(bounds, n, skip, seed)` adds one uniform random vector, drawn from `seed`, to every unit point modulo 1 before scaling.
This is the randomisation of Cranley and Patterson [2].
Each shift keeps the low discrepancy of the design, different seeds give independent replicas, and the spread of an estimate over replicas measures its error.
The shift comes from a seeded `StdRng`, so a seed gives the same points with the same build of the crate; a new version of `rand` may change them.

### Anchored designs

A Halton design after point 0 never contains a corner of the box, and an optimum on the boundary is then reached only by clipping.
`boundary_anchored_low_discrepancy_points` overwrites the first rows: with room for them, the `2^d` corners followed by the centre, and otherwise `low`, `high` and the centre.
The other rows keep their Halton values, so the design remains well spread inside the box.

### References

The implementation:

- R. Goswami, eindir, Zenodo. [doi:10.5281/zenodo.10672737](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10672737)

The methods:

1. J. H. Halton, "On the efficiency of certain quasi-random sequences of points in evaluating multi-dimensional integrals", Numer. Math. 2, 84-90 (1960). [doi:10.1007/BF01386213](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01386213)
2. R. Cranley and T. N. L. Patterson, "Randomization of Number Theoretic Methods for Multiple Integration", SIAM J. Numer. Anal. 13, 904-914 (1976). [doi:10.1137/0713071](https://doi.org/10.1137/0713071)

## The GLE thermostat

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/explanation/gle.org

### The problem it solves

Langevin dynamics samples the Boltzmann distribution by adding friction and noise to Hamiltonian dynamics.
With white noise there is one friction constant `gamma`, and a harmonic mode of frequency `omega` decorrelates fastest near critical damping, when `gamma` is of order `omega`.
An ill-conditioned objective has curvatures, and so frequencies, spread over orders of magnitude, and one `gamma` leaves most of them over- or under-damped.

The generalized Langevin equation (GLE) replaces the single friction by a memory kernel.
Ceriotti, Bussi and Parrinello showed that a kernel built from a few auxiliary momenta, coupled linearly to the physical momentum, gives a Markovian system that can be integrated exactly and tuned so that the friction, and with it the sampling efficiency, is nearly flat over a chosen band of frequencies [1, 2].

### What eindir computes

For each coordinate, the state is a vector `s` of `ns + 1` entries: the mass-scaled physical momentum in `s[0]` and `ns` auxiliary momenta.
Its dynamics is the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process `ds = -A s dt + B dW`, with drift matrix `A` and diffusion matrix `B`.
The exact solution over one step `dt` is

```text
s <- T s + S xi,   T = exp(-dt A),   S S^T = kb (C - T C T^T),
```

with `xi` standard normal and `C` the stationary covariance.
`GleThermostat::new` computes `T` with `matrix_exp` (Taylor series with scaling and squaring) and `S` with `ldl_sqrt`, a pivoted LDL^T square root that tolerates the nearly singular matrix that small `dt` produces.
These follow the `ThermoGLE` propagator of i-PI [3].
Neither needs a linear-algebra library, because the matrices have only `ns + 1` rows.

### Correctness from C, speed from A

The stationary distribution of the process is `N(0, kb C)`, whatever the drift.
Setting `C = temperature * I`, as `GleThermostat::canonical` does, makes the physical momentum Boltzmann-distributed for any valid `A`.
The drift only decides how fast each frequency decorrelates.
This is the decoupling of correctness from efficiency that Ceriotti, Bussi and Parrinello call colored-noise thermostats "à la carte" [2], and it is why one drift matrix can be reused at every temperature.

### The optimal-sampling drift

`optimal_sampling_drift(omega0)` returns a fitted `A` with six damped-oscillator baths, each a pair of auxiliary momenta with eigenvalues `-Gamma ± i Omega`, skew-coupled to the physical momentum.
Spreading the bath frequencies over the band `[omega0, 100 omega0]` flattens the friction across it.
The parameters were fitted to maximise the worst normalised sampling efficiency over the band, following the procedure of the GLE input generator at [gle4md.org](https://gle4md.org); the fit lives in `experiments/colored_noise_sampling.py` of anneal.
Since `A` has units of frequency, scaling the band only multiplies the matrix by `omega0`.

The symmetric part `A + A^T` of this matrix is diagonal and non-negative, so with `C = I` the fluctuation-dissipation relation `A C + C A^T = B B^T` has a real solution `B`, and the canonical thermostat is valid.

### Who uses it

The GLE Langevin driver of [anneal](https://github.com/HaoZeke/anneal) builds the thermostat once, draws the initial auxiliary state with `sample_stationary`, and calls `step` between force kicks.
The objective values and the accept decisions stay in anneal.

### References

The implementation and the fitted drift:

- R. Goswami, eindir, Zenodo. [doi:10.5281/zenodo.10672737](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10672737)
- R. Goswami, R. Goswami, A. Goswami, M. Sallermann, S. Goswami and D. Goswami, "anneal_repro: reproducibility harness for Typed Component Algebras for Simulated Annealing and Markov-Chain Monte Carlo", version 0.4.0, Zenodo (2026). [doi:10.5281/zenodo.20672621](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20672621)

The method:

1. M. Ceriotti, G. Bussi and M. Parrinello, "Langevin Equation with Colored Noise for Constant-Temperature Molecular Dynamics Simulations", Phys. Rev. Lett. 102, 020601 (2009). [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.102.020601](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.102.020601)
2. M. Ceriotti, G. Bussi and M. Parrinello, "Colored-Noise Thermostats à la Carte", J. Chem. Theory Comput. 6, 1170-1180 (2010). [doi:10.1021/ct900563s](https://doi.org/10.1021/ct900563s)
3. M. Ceriotti, J. More and D. E. Manolopoulos, "i-PI: A Python interface for ab initio path integral molecular dynamics simulations", Comput. Phys. Commun. 185, 1019-1026 (2014). [doi:10.1016/j.cpc.2013.10.027](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cpc.2013.10.027)

## Surrogates

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/explanation/surrogates.org

A surrogate is a cheap model of the objective, fitted on a pilot design.
eindir has three: an additive model in all coordinates, a polynomial on a few directions, and a wrapper that restricts an objective to those directions.
All three implement `Objective`, so a driver can use them wherever it takes an objective, and a sampler can use them for proposals while it still accepts or rejects with the true objective.

### The additive surrogate

`AdditiveSurrogate` models `f(x) ≈ c + sum_j g_j(x_j)`, with each `g_j` a Chebyshev series in one coordinate.
This is a generalized additive model [1], and Chebyshev series are a natural basis for smooth functions on an interval [2].
In the language of tensor trains it is a rank-1 functional tensor train over all `d` coordinates.

`fit` sets `c` to the pilot mean and refits one coordinate at a time against the residual of the others (backfitting, [1]), 12 passes by default.
Each coordinate's columns are centred on their pilot means, because under uniform sampling the even Chebyshev polynomials have nonzero mean and an uncentred fit would leak into `c`.
A pass costs one small solve per coordinate with a cached factor, so the fit is linear in `d`.

### Independence proposals

The tempered density `exp(-f(x) / T)` of an additive model factorises into one density per coordinate.
`sample` draws each coordinate by inverse CDF on a grid, which costs `O(d m)` for a grid of `m` nodes, and one draw puts every coordinate near its own tempered optimum at once.
When `f` is separable this is an exact draw from the surrogate's tempered law; when it is not, the proposal is biased toward the additive part, and a Metropolis-Hastings accept step on the true objective removes the bias.
The additive independence driver of anneal works this way.

### Reduced objectives and active subspaces

Many functions of many variables vary mostly along a few directions.
Active subspace methods find them from the eigenvectors of the average outer product of the gradient [3].
`ReducedObjective::new(inner, origin, basis, bounds)` evaluates `inner` at `origin + basis r`, so a driver can search the low-dimensional `r` instead of `x`.
The point is clipped to the bounds of `inner` before evaluation, and the gradient is `basis^T ∇f` with the clipped components of `∇f` set to zero.
eindir does not compute the basis; the caller supplies it.
`ChebyshevSurrogate` is a total-degree Chebyshev polynomial with value and gradient, for a cheap model on the reduced box; the caller supplies its terms and coefficients.

### References

The implementation and its use in samplers:

- R. Goswami, eindir, Zenodo. [doi:10.5281/zenodo.10672737](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10672737)
- R. Goswami, R. Goswami, A. Goswami, M. Sallermann, S. Goswami and D. Goswami, "anneal_repro: reproducibility harness for Typed Component Algebras for Simulated Annealing and Markov-Chain Monte Carlo", version 0.4.0, Zenodo (2026). [doi:10.5281/zenodo.20672621](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20672621)

The methods:

1. T. Hastie and R. Tibshirani, "Generalized Additive Models", Stat. Sci. 1, 297-310 (1986). [doi:10.1214/ss/1177013604](https://doi.org/10.1214/ss/1177013604)
2. L. N. Trefethen, *Approximation Theory and Approximation Practice, Extended Edition*, SIAM (2019). [doi:10.1137/1.9781611975949](https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9781611975949)
3. P. G. Constantine, E. Dow and Q. Wang, "Active Subspace Methods in Theory and Practice: Applications to Kriging Surfaces", SIAM J. Sci. Comput. 36, A1500-A1524 (2014). [doi:10.1137/130916138](https://doi.org/10.1137/130916138)

## Fallible objectives

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/explanation/fallible-objectives.org

### The problem

`Objective::eval` and `Gradient::grad` return a value, not a `Result`.
A potential energy surface that can fail (the engine returns an error, the geometry has a non-finite coordinate, the engine refuses the configuration) can only panic or return a sentinel such as NaN.
The sentinel loses the reason, and a panic cannot cross a C boundary.
A driver that receives a C objective through `EindirObjectiveWrapper` sees a failed evaluation only as NaN, with no status and no message.

The fallible path is additive.
`Objective`, `Gradient` and `DifferentiableObjective` are unchanged, and so is the C callback ABI of `eindir_objective_t`.

### The traits

| Trait | Methods | Error type |
|---|---|---|
| `TryObjective<T>` | `dims`, `domain`, `try_eval`, `try_eval_batch`, `known_min` | `Error` |
| `TryGradient<T>` | `try_grad`, `grad_dims` | `GradError` |
| `TryDifferentiableObjective<T>` | `try_value_and_gradient` | both, equal |

Each error type is the implementor's own.
Nothing boxes it, converts it or wraps it, so a function generic over `O: TryDifferentiableObjective<f64>` returns `O::Error` exactly as the objective produced it.

#### Blanket impls

Every `Objective<T>` is a `TryObjective<T>` with `Error = core::convert::Infallible`, every `Gradient<T>` is a `TryGradient<T>` with `GradError = Infallible`, and every `DifferentiableObjective<T>` is a `TryDifferentiableObjective<T>`.
The blanket impls call the infallible methods, so an overridden `eval_batch`, `global_min` or fused `value_and_gradient` is kept.
A driver written against the `Try*` traits therefore accepts both kinds of objective, and for an infallible one the error branch is statically unreachable: `match e {}` on an `Infallible` needs no arm.

A type that implements `Objective` must not implement `TryObjective` by hand, since the blanket impl already covers it.
A type that does not implement `Objective` can implement `TryObjective` freely: a downstream crate's own type does not overlap with the blanket impl, and `tests/fallible.rs` checks that from outside the crate.

#### Names

The methods are `dims`, `domain` and `grad_dims`, not `dim`, `bounds` and `dim`.
Because of the blanket impls an infallible type is also a `Try*` type, and equal names would make `x.dim()` ambiguous (E0034) wherever both traits are in scope.

The gradient's error is `GradError` so that `O::Error` is unambiguous for a driver bounded by `TryDifferentiableObjective`.
Two associated types both called `Error` in the two supertraits would make `O::Error` fail with E0221, and the driver would have to write `<O as TryObjective<f64>>::Error`.
A trait object spells both: `dyn TryDifferentiableObjective<f64, Error = E, GradError = E>`.

### Adapters

| Direction | Item | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| infallible to fallible | blanket impls | `Ok(eval(x))`, with `Infallible` |
| fallible to infallible | `NanOnError::new(inner, sink)` | NaN for a failed value or gradient; every error goes to `sink` first |
| fallible to infallible | `PanicOnError::new(inner)` | panics with a message naming the call and the `Debug` form of the error, for tests and scripts |
| closure | `TryOracle::new(bounds, f)` | `f: x -> Result<(f, grad), E>`, one call for both |
| value only to gradient | `TryFiniteDiffGradient::new(obj)` | central differences over a `TryObjective`; stops at the first error |
| batch | `try_eval_batch_parallel` | Rayon above `EVAL_BATCH_PARALLEL_MIN`; the lowest failing row's error |

`NanOnError` is the existing sentinel convention with the error kept: the sink can log the error, count it, or store the first one.

### C callbacks

`eindir_objective_t` is untouched: same callbacks, same layout (still layout 3), same `eindir_status_t`.
The fallible form is a second handle, `eindir_try_objective_t`, because adding callback fields to the first would change its size and break every embedder.

```c
typedef int32_t (*EindirTryEvalFn)(void *user_data,
                                   const struct DLManagedTensorVersioned *x,
                                   double *value_out,
                                   char *message_out, uintptr_t message_cap);
```

- The callback returns `0` for success and any other value for failure, and writes a NUL-terminated message into the buffer eindir lends it (`EINDIR_TRY_MESSAGE_CAP` bytes, never NULL).
  Statuses `1` and `2` mean invalid parameter and internal error, and the others belong to the callback.
- `eindir_try_objective_eval` and `eindir_try_objective_grad` return the callback's status, copy the message into the caller's buffer (truncated to fit, and NULL is allowed) and also record it for `eindir_last_error()`.
  The old entry points leave `eindir_last_error()` alone after a callback fails, and these do not.
- A callback's message reaches `CallbackError`, `eindir_last_error()` and `message_out` as valid UTF-8 that keeps every byte.
  Valid UTF-8 is copied as it is except that each backslash is doubled, and each byte that is not valid UTF-8 becomes `\xhh` in lowercase hexadecimal, so the bytes up to the first NUL can be recovered.
  Escaping makes a message longer, and `message_out` truncates it to `message_cap`; `CallbackError` and `eindir_last_error()` keep all of it.
- In Rust, `EindirTryObjectiveWrapper` implements the `Try*` traits with `Error = CallbackError { code, message }`, so a failure reaches a generic driver with both fields intact.
  Without a gradient callback `try_grad` fails with "no gradient callback"; the old wrapper returns zeros.
- `eindir_core_abi_stamp()` reports ABI minor 2 and the feature bit `EINDIR_ABI_FEATURE_TRY_CALLBACKS`.
  A consumer built against minor 1 still passes `eindir_core_abi_compatible`.

### Writing a driver against the fallible traits

A driver keeps the objective's error type as a type parameter instead of converting it.
One way is an enum with a variant for the driver's own failures and one for the objective's:

```rust
#[non_exhaustive]
pub enum StepError<E> {
    /// The driver's own failure, such as a collapsed trust region.
    Solver(SolverError),
    /// The objective's error, exactly as it returned it.
    Objective(E),
}

pub fn try_step<O>(obj: &O, x: &mut Array1<f64>) -> Result<Report, StepError<O::Error>>
where
    O: TryDifferentiableObjective<f64> + ?Sized;
```

An infallible entry point can then call `try_step` and remove the `Objective` variant with `match e {}`, since its `E` is `Infallible`.
The nested form `Result<Result<Report, SolverError>, E>` also passes `E` through unchanged, but `?` cannot unwrap both levels.

Put no bound on `E` (no `std::error::Error`, `Debug` or `Send`) beyond what the driver calls, so that any error type fits.
Decide what a failure leaves behind: the simplest contract is that a failed step leaves the point and the driver's memory as they were before the call, as a non-finite value would.
A failure at a trial point of a line search is the objective refusing that point; a driver can stop with it, or let the caller pass a predicate `Fn(&E) -> bool` for errors that should count as an uphill trial instead.

[Objectives that can fail](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/howto/fallible.org) has a complete program.

## The C ABI

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/explanation/c-abi.org

The C ABI lets code in any language that can call C hand an objective to Rust drivers, and lets C code evaluate objectives that eindir created.
This page explains its parts and the choices behind them.
[Objectives through the C ABI](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaoZeke/eindir/main/docs/orgmode/howto/c-objective.org) shows how to use it.

### Two handles

`eindir_objective_t` is a plain C struct: the dimension, pointers to the bounds, a value callback, an optional gradient callback, an opaque `user_data` pointer with an optional destructor, and an optional descriptor pointer.
Because it is `#[repr(C)]` and holds no Rust types, a producer can put it first in a struct of its own and pass a pointer to that struct where a handle is expected; the cast costs nothing.
A handle from `eindir_objective_new` owns copies of the bounds and is freed by `eindir_objective_free`.
An embedded handle belongs to its producer, which frees it.
